newsitem.title: USA: Economics loom over future of nuclear power.
newsitem.headline: Economics loom over future of nuclear power.

text.p: Nuclear power, once lauded as the fuel of the future and later vilified as an environmental time bomb, may be facing its deadliest foe yet: economic annihilation.

A proposal Wednesday by Connecticut Yankee Atomic Power Co. to shut down its reactor at Haddam Neck, Conn., is being cited by industry analysts as the most recent example of the troubled industry's vulnerability to market deregulation.
"It's not surprising that several of these plants probably are going to be shut down," said Ed Rothschild, director of energy policy at Citizen's Action, a consumer advocacy group in Washington.
"In a competitive market, if you deny utilities the right to pass on the cost of these plants, they are too expensive to operate. They never should never have been built in the first place," he said.
However, proponents of nuclear power do not see Connecticut Yankee as a harbinger of things to come.

"We think this is an isolated incident. There are no signs that any other U.S. plants are looking at the same course of action," said Scott Peterson, a spokesman for the Nuclear Energy Institute, also in Washington.

But no one denies the heavy role government played in fostering the nuclear industry, or that the safety net beneath it is being slowly pulled away by Federal Energy Regulatory Commission efforts to deregulate the market.

"Connecticut Yankee was built under the protection of regulation and supported by regulation. Now nuclear plants are no longer economical at selling power into a competitive market," said Raymond Moore, securities analyst at Dillon Read in New York.
"The success of these plants depended on their economy of scale. What we've had is just the opposite. Small (generating) units can be built at overall rates much cheaper," he said.

Smaller units -- fired by natural gas, coal or oil -- are easier to finance, more quickly built, and less burdened by the environmental and safety regulations that have halted the construction of new nuclear power plants in this country.

They are also at the core of deregulation, whose basic tenant is to cut the cost of power to consumers by taking advantage of the nation's surplus generating capacity -- estimated at 20 percent more than actual demand for electricity.

Bruce Kenyon, president and chief executive officer of the Connecticut Yankee Atomic Power Co., said the board's recommendation to close the plant was based on a review of operations, expenses, and the cost of replacement power.
The board concluded the plant faced an "economic disadvantage" that ranged from "tens of millions of dollars to as high as $100 million."
Utilities, recognising their survival in an open market depends on cost-efficiency and adequate returns to shareholders, are now openly saying they cannot carry this kind of load.

A final decision on closing Connecticut Yankee likely will be taken next month by its owners, a consortium of New England utilities and municipalities led by Northeast Utilities, which holds a 49 percent stake in the 582 megawatt facility.
The replacement power Kenyon referred to is already available in a growing spot market that did not exist when most of the country's 110 nuclear power plants were conceived 20 to 30 years ago.
